narrative.text: Krel reports a massive success. His anti-corruption task force raided a company funding Orythian spies and seized ₭ 5 million in black-market assets. But Danika Oberlin storms into your study right after he leaves, looking furious.

Chancellor, I ran the background checks on the company Krel just raided. They weren't spies. 'Thorne Imports' is a legitimate Lytheirian textile firm. Krel planted the Orythian cipher codes in their files to justify the seizure.

He framed an innocent company to steal ₭ 5 million for the state treasury? That is not justice, Chancellor. That is state-sponsored piracy. And if the Lytheirian Ambassador finds out, it is an international incident.
It's the ghost payroll again. Four administrators vanished on Krel's word in week eighty-six. You told me the investigation was ongoing. It wasn't. This is what he learned from that.
Week sixty-six. I sent him to a warehouse I had just sat in, to make a point to Stefan Morvec. He made it. He has been making points for me ever since.
In week seventy-two I told him: no record, no arrests, just silence. He has given me silence ever since. I am only now hearing what it sounds like.

Krel has lost his mind. Or maybe he has just become exactly what I created him to be: a man who will do anything to protect the Republic. The money is real, and the treasury needs it. But he committed a crime against a foreign nation and framed innocent businessmen. If I expose him, I lose my best agent and face a massive scandal. If I cover it up, I am complicit in theft.

choices.text: Cover it up. Keep the money. Protect Krel.
Return the money to Lytheira and apologize. Reprimand Krel.
Arrest Krel's men for the frame-up. Prove to Lytheira it was rogue agents.

narrative.text: The money stays in the treasury, which needs it. Krel receives a private meeting with me — no record, no witnesses — in which I tell him what I know and what I am choosing not to do about it. He nods once. He understands the transaction: I own this now, which means he owes me something neither of us will name. The Lytheirian firm files a complaint with the Assembly of Nations three weeks later. We deny everything. Oberlin handles the paperwork. She signs it without speaking to me for four days afterward.

The money is returned with an official letter of apology and a formal reprimand filed in Krel's personnel record — a document that will never surface publicly and which he knows I could make disappear if I chose to. The Lytheirian Ambassador accepts the return with what he calls 'measured satisfaction.' Krel says nothing about the reprimand. He continues his work. The personnel record sits in the file. I know it exists. He knows I know. We have reached the particular kind of understanding that passes for trust between a Chancellor and her intelligence chief.

Three of Krel's field agents are arrested and charged as rogue operatives acting without authorization. The evidence is genuine — they did act without explicit authorization on paper, which is how Krel structures everything. Krel watches the proceedings from a distance and says nothing publicly. The Lytheirian Ambassador is satisfied. Krel is intact. The three men are convicted of a crime they committed on orders that no record will ever show. I signed a letter saying I did not know. Both of those sentences are true, depending on how you define 'know.'
